source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping - Exp 1 (matching)
finding: When people judge which facts belong in an analogy, they prefer a fact tied into a shared causal system over an equally good isolated match. Control readers who saw only the target showed no such preference, so it is not a salience artefact.
numbers: Exp 1: 48 undergraduates (24 analogy, 24 target-only). Choice task: mean shared-system choices out of 4 passages 3.17 (analogy) vs 2.0 (target-only), F(1,44)=18.43, p<.001. Per passage analogy group chose shared-system fact 67-92%, controls 42-54%; Fisher exact significant for 3 of 4 passages.
limits: Four hand-built science-style passages; one pair of key facts each; students; paid. Shows preference in judging, not accuracy of inferences.
agent_relevance: A mapping step should favour matches that sit inside a connected relational system. Isolated look-alike facts should not be trusted as support for a transfer.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping - Exp 2 (predictions)
finding: Asked to predict a missing fact about the target, analogy subjects mostly predicted the base fact that followed from the shared causal system, not an equally plausible base fact that would be an isolated match. Target-only controls rarely produced either, so the prediction came from the analogy.
numbers: Exp 2: 32 undergraduates, 16 per group. Share of predictions: shared-system fact .53, different-system fact .12, other .27 (analogy); shared .12, different .12, other .74 (target-only). About .08 of responses predicted both and were dropped. Inter-rater agreement .88 before discussion.
limits: Only two candidate facts offered by design. Over a quarter of analogy responses projected neither planted fact. Inference quality was never checked against ground truth.
agent_relevance: Direct human support for the rule used in candidate-inference selection: project facts that are connected to already-mapped structure. This is the property a code check of an O7 transfer can test.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping - Exp 3 (predictions, replication with changed materials)
finding: Exp 3 repeated the prediction task with altered materials and got the same pattern, with a larger share of different-system predictions than in Exp 2.
numbers: Exp 3: 48 undergraduates, 24 per group. Analogy group overall: shared-system .53, different-system .22. Target-only group: mostly 'other' predictions (.62 to .96 by passage). Inter-rater agreement .96. About .07 of responses predicted both and were dropped. Per-passage shared-system rate in analogy group ranged .375 to .75.
limits: Same lab, same design family, same population. No independent replication in this file.
agent_relevance: The systematicity preference is repeatable but far from absolute: about 1 in 5 predictions followed the unsupported fact. Expect a minority of candidate inferences to be unsupported even when the mapping is good.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity, American Psychologist - candidate inferences are guesses; convergent human findings
finding: The review states that structure mapping projects unmatched base facts as candidate inferences, and that these are only guesses that can be false. It lists convergent human results: people predicted the fact linked to the matching causal antecedent more than twice as often as the other fact (Clement and Gentner), with convergent findings from Read 1984, Spellman and Holyoak, Markman 1996 and Lassaline 1996 (willingness to infer a new property in category induction rose when it linked to shared causal relations).
numbers: No new numbers. Cited result: more than twice as often for the connected key fact (Clement and Gentner 1991).
limits: Secondary summary. The cited Lassaline, Markman and Spellman and Holyoak papers were not opened this session (see the opened:false line).
agent_relevance: The design rule for O7 is transfer, then test: a candidate inference is a hypothesis, not a fact.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity, American Psychologist - direction of inference and coherence of base
finding: Inference flows from the more systematic, causally coherent item (the base) to the less coherent one (the target). Bowdle and Gentner found people preferred the coherent passage as base, generated more inferences from it, and rated such comparisons more informative. A second result: mapping that extends an existing connected mapping is read faster than starting a new mapping, but only for novel metaphors, not conventional ones.
numbers: No figures given in the review for these effects.
limits: Review text only; the primary papers (Bowdle and Gentner; Forbus et al.; Keane et al.) were not opened.
agent_relevance: Pick the richer, better-explained case as the source and the poorer case as the target. Do not transfer from a source whose causal structure is thinner than the target's.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein & Thompson (2003) Learning and transfer: a general role for analogical encoding - Exp 1 and 2
finding: Comparing two cases made novices far more likely to use the shared principle on a new problem than reading the same cases separately. Guided analogy beat no training. Learners did not compare spontaneously even when cases were side by side.
numbers: Exp 1: guided analogy 15/32 (47%) transferred vs 6% baseline, chi2(1,N=48)=7.92, p<.01. Exp 2: N=128; comparison condition 48% transferred vs 19% separate cases, chi2(1,N=128)=11.85, p<.01. Comparison participants linked cases 98% vs 16%, chi2=89.55.
limits: Negotiation contract principles (trade-off, contingent contract); undergraduates; the effect was larger for trade-offs than for contingent contracts. Written solutions, not real stakes in Exp 1-2.
agent_relevance: Strong human evidence that the act of explicitly aligning two cases is what gets the inference out. A scaffold that makes the model state the shared structure before it transfers has human support.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein & Thompson (2003) Learning and transfer: a general role for analogical encoding - Exp 3 (face-to-face, dose of comparison support)
finding: More support for comparing cases gave more transfer in live two-person negotiations, in a graded way.
numbers: Exp 3: N=158 (20 dyads per condition, 19 for baseline). Contingent contracts formed: guided analogy 90% (18/20), comparison 70%, separate cases 55%, baseline 37%. Participants who suggested a contingency as ideal: 73% guided, 68% comparison, 48% separate, 47% baseline, chi2(1,N=158)=8.30.
limits: Dyad outcome depends on the partner too. Single domain. One test case.
agent_relevance: Dose-response: stated mapping plus a supporting definition and diagram is better than a bare instruction to compare. Fits a typed mapping with a written rule.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1980, 1983) analogical problem solving (radiation problem)
finding: Classic result, taken here from memory and from the 2025 Puranam paper: unaided analogue use is rare and a hint to use the earlier story raises it a lot.
numbers: From the Puranam et al. account of Gick and Holyoak 1983 Exp 2: 29% (8/28) solved without a hint, 50% (14/28) with a hint. Original 1980 spontaneous rate from memory: about 10%; with hint about 90% (not verified this session).
limits: Not opened. Numbers for 1980 are recalled and unverified. Publisher page returned HTTP 403.
agent_relevance: Supports the schema's note that unaided analogy rarely transfers. The hint is the operator: force the is-there-an-analogue step.

source: Alfieri, Nokes-Malach & Schunn (2013) Learning through case comparisons: a meta-analytic review, Educational Psychologist
finding: Meta-analysis of case-comparison learning across studies; reported a moderate positive effect of comparing cases over studying them separately, larger when comparison is guided.
numbers: From memory: overall effect about d = 0.50 across about 57 studies. Not verified this session.
limits: Not opened (web search and Semantic Scholar rate-limited, publisher 403). Treat numbers as to-be-checked.
agent_relevance: If confirmed, gives a pooled effect size to set against the single-lab 48% vs 19% of Gentner et al.

source: Lassaline (1996); Spellman & Holyoak (1996); Markman (1997) - human inference constraints
finding: Cited by Gentner and Markman 1997 as convergent evidence that people project inferences along connected causal structure. Spellman and Holyoak also show that goals and pragmatics change which mapping people build.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: None of the three were opened. Known only through the secondary account in the Gentner and Markman line. Markman 1997 URL on the Northwestern site returned 404.
agent_relevance: Pragmatic goals shape the mapping, so a scaffold should state the goal before mapping.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour - story analogies and letter-string/matrix tasks
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on text matrix and letter-string analogy tasks, but on story analogies (causal structure, Gentner et al. materials) students clearly beat it. GPT-3 was not significant in the far (cross-domain) condition.
numbers: Story analogies: humans N=54, GPT-3 vs humans OR=0.37, p=0.0003; 15/54 humans picked the analogous story on every trial. Near condition GPT-3 binomial p=0.0039; far condition p=0.065 (not significant). Letter-string: N=57 humans, GPT-3 better overall, OR=1.76, p=6.3e-5, mostly on zero-generalisation problems. Digit matrices N=40, OR=1.88, p=0.005. GPT-4 informal check: near perfect on near analogies, stronger on far.
limits: Undergraduate sample; GPT-3 only for main tests; training-data contamination cannot be excluded (see the replication lines).
agent_relevance: Sensitivity to higher-order causal relations is weaker in older models and improves with scale; the far (cross-domain) case is where inference is least reliable.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour - Gick & Holyoak style problem solving (qualitative)
finding: GPT-3 behaved like humans on the radiation problem: alone it proposed injecting the source into the tumour; after the general story it gave the convergence solution; with two distractor stories it dropped back; when told to consider earlier stories it recovered.
numbers: Single qualitative runs (Supplementary S5.1-S5.5), no counts. Same pattern on the genie/gumball problem from a developmental study.
limits: One prompt per condition, no sampling statistics, a famous problem likely in the training data.
agent_relevance: Same weak point as humans: the analogue is found only when cued. A required check-earlier-material step is the cheap fix.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: A failed generalisation of Webb et al.: on letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets, humans stayed high while GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 dropped sharply. Counterfactual comprehension checks showed models understood the altered alphabets, so the drop is not just confusion.
numbers: Humans: 136 recruited on Prolific, 1,876 samples. Mean accuracy: humans .753, GPT-3 .488, GPT-3.5 .350, GPT-4 .452 (6,840 samples per model). Error types: alternate valid rule 38.6% of human errors, 22% GPT-4, 5.8% GPT-3; incorrect-rule 31% GPT-3 and 33% GPT-4 vs 15% humans. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were not better than GPT-3.
limits: Letter-string domain only; human accuracy here (.75) above the original study's humans. A later reply argues the drop reflects a counting weakness.
agent_relevance: Transfer of a rule to altered surface forms is the weak spot. Test any transfer step on a counterfactual variant of the source, not only on the familiar form.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (reply)
finding: Authors' reply: the degraded performance on the permuted-alphabet, larger-interval task comes from difficulty counting letter positions. GPT-4 given code execution, which it used unprompted to convert letters to indices, solved the counterfactual problems at roughly human level.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). Of GPT-4 errors, 46% (23/50) used a valid alternative rule vs 39% in the human data of Lewis and Mitchell. A second counterfactual task gave similar results (Supp S2.4).
limits: Authors defending their own result. The counting explanation is an alternative reading, not a decisive test. Code is not a human-like solution.
agent_relevance: A tool (code) removes a mechanical bottleneck without changing the analogical step. Use code for the mapping and checking, as the schema already proposes.

source: Hodel & West (2023/2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: A failed replication: simple variants of the original letter-string tasks (synthetic alphabet, larger interval) pushed GPT-3 close to zero while humans stayed high.
numbers: GPT-3 generative accuracy below 0.1 on extend-sequence, successor/predecessor and fix-alphabetic-sequence with the synthetic alphabet and larger interval; accuracy comparable to the original only for remove-redundant-letter and sort. N=50 instances per condition. Counterfactual comprehension check: at least 30% of original level on all but one condition.
limits: Letter-string only; GPT-3 (davinci) not later models. The remove and sort tasks do not need generating letters, which weakens the contamination reading.
agent_relevance: Do not accept zero-shot analogy claims without altered-surface tests.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR
finding: Telling the model to recall relevant problems and solve them first (self-generated exemplars) beat 0-shot and fixed few-shot chain of thought on maths, code and BIG-Bench. Adding a self-generated knowledge step helped most on hard code tasks, because it made recalled problems share the algorithm instead of surface words.
numbers: Average accuracy gain +4% over baselines. GSM8K (GPT-3.5-turbo) about 75-78% across methods, small gains; MATH gain larger. Codeforces Acc@1: GPT-3.5-turbo with the method 15% vs GPT-4 16%. K=5 exemplars for GSM8K, K=3 for MATH and BIG-Bench; temperature 0.
limits: Gains are small on easy tasks (GSM8K) and larger on hard ones. No check that recalled problems are correct. Table text was garbled in extraction, so per-cell numbers were not used.
agent_relevance: O7 can start from the model's own recalled problems with no retrieval store, but this recalls whole solutions, not a checked mapping.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR - scale and retrieval comparison
finding: Self-generated exemplars help more with stronger models. With smaller or weaker models, retrieving labelled exemplars from a training set is better, because generated exemplars may be invalid. Without the knowledge step, recalled exemplars follow lexical similarity (for example palindromes) rather than the needed algorithm.
numbers: GSM8K scale table (text-curie-001 to text-davinci-003; 0-shot, 0-shot CoT, 5-shot fixed, 5-shot retrieved, self-generated): self-generation best at the largest scale; retrieved CoT best at smaller scales. davinci-003 5-shot retrieved CoT 54% vs fixed 50%.
limits: Exact cell values uncertain from the extracted table; the direction of the result is stated in the paper's text.
agent_relevance: Generated analogues are only as good as the model's own knowledge. For weak models, give retrieved or curated analogues.

source: Yu, He & Ying (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs, ICLR - shortest path
finding: Solving the input plus several analogous (neighbouring) problems and reusing their results beat plain, CoT and Tree-of-Thought prompting on optimal-path rate, with the largest gain on the weaker model. ToT did worse than plain prompting for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 at 0-shot because of accumulated errors.
numbers: 100 shortest-path problems. Optimal rate 0-shot: PaLM-2 IO .14, CoT .24, TP .36; GPT-3.5 IO .33, CoT .26, ToT .22, TP .65; GPT-4 IO .78, CoT .76, ToT .46, TP .88. Over-length rate GPT-4 TP .05 vs IO .10. Gain of 5-shot over 1-shot small or negative. 2-layer TP gave only marginal gain over 1-layer at more tokens.
limits: Synthetic graph task where sub-problems have exact structure (neighbour nodes); not a test of cross-domain candidate inferences. Aggregation step is done by the LLM.
agent_relevance: Reusing solved neighbouring problems works when the analogy is exact and the sub-answers can be combined. Cheap on tasks with decomposable structure.

source: Yu, He & Ying (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs, ICLR - creative writing and ALFWorld planning
finding: On ALFWorld, planning with solutions from analogous tasks raised the completion rate over ReAct and Reflexion; on creative writing it raised coherence and human preference.
numbers: ALFWorld 134 unseen environments, All-task success: ReAct avg 57, ReAct best of 6 71, Reflexion 79.1 (reproduced), TP variants 83.68 to 94.78. Creative writing: 100 instances, 5 analogous problems, 6 plans aggregated; TP top coherence score and user preference for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Abstract claims +15% planning completion, +13% human preference.
limits: Baseline numbers other than Reflexion are quoted from earlier papers, not re-run. Compute is larger (6 plans). Row labels for TP variants not fully recoverable from the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Evidence that carrying a plan from a nearby solved case helps agents, at extra compute cost.

source: Puranam, Sen & Workiewicz (2025) Can LLMs help improve analogical reasoning for strategic decisions? Humans and GPT-4
finding: Matching is the weak step. With two source stories and two target problems, GPT-4 recalled almost every relevant analogy but also applied wrong ones (low precision). Humans applied few but mostly the right ones. A hint to use an analogy lifted both groups.
numbers: 199 students vs 60 GPT-4 runs (15 per cell). Humans solved HR problem 37% (17/46) with hint vs 20.3% without; factory problem 8.7% (4/46) vs 6.3%. Gick and Holyoak 1983 baseline: 29% (8/28) vs 50% (14/28). GPT-4 used an analogy in 1/15 factory runs without hint, 15/15 with hint; HR 14/15 without. With hint GPT-4 recall 1.00, precision about .50 (F1 .67-.68); humans precision .67-.75, recall .26-.39, F1 .38-.51. Without hint humans' recall .06 (radiation) and .22 (dolphin).
limits: Preprint; business vignettes; small GPT-4 cells; the no-hint confusion-matrix table was inconsistent in the extracted text, so only the stated summary was used. Matching two sources to two targets is harder than the original one-to-one design.
agent_relevance: The LLM mapping step over-applies analogies on surface similarity. Add an explicit relational check or an independent verifier before a candidate inference is acted on (fits G8: generator does not select).

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: story-level analogies from LLMs
finding: Choosing the analogous story from four options was hard for LLMs: they were drawn to surface-similar hard negatives instead of the structurally analogous story. A structure-aware retrieval baseline was more resistant.
numbers: 24K story pairs, annotated for entity and relational similarity. Multiple choice: humans 85.7%, random 25%, text-davinci-003 average 37.1%, GPT-3.5 33-44% by shot count, ChatGPT 29-36%, FlanT5-xxl 45-46%, LLaMa-65B 28-48%, Sultan and Shahaf retrieval baseline 44.9%. Easy (random) negatives were chosen under 20% of the time, so models use surface cues. More demonstrations gave no consistent gain; naming creative analogy or giving a Structure-Mapping definition helped.
limits: 2023 models. Annotators judged similarity from text; stories partly LLM-generated.
agent_relevance: Do not trust an LLM to pick the best analogue by feel. Score structure with code and use surface-matched distractors to test the scaffold.

source: Sourati et al. (2023/2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Models spot near (same-domain) analogies but fail on far analogies where surface overlap is low; GPT-4 was below chance on far analogies zero-shot. Solved examples and chain of thought helped, but the best model closed only about half the gap to humans.
numbers: Binary task, random baseline 50%. Humans: near analogies 97.9%, far analogies 94.1%, average about 96%. Models: average about 57%, far analogies 39.6% on average (below chance). Benchmark has 4 far/near analogy/disanalogy categories.
limits: Narratives with a proverb-level message; classification, not inference generation. Few-shot gains partial.
agent_relevance: Far analogues are where an LLM judge is least reliable, consistent with the schema's advice to use them only at impasses and under code checks.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) Beneath surface similarity: LLMs make reasonable scientific analogies after structure abduction (SCAR)
finding: Word-analogy accuracy overstates analogical skill. LLMs that score near humans on word analogy still struggle to identify the relational structure and map concepts across two scientific systems.
numbers: SCAR: 400 scientific analogies from 13 fields, 1,614 concept mappings. GPT-4 reached human level on most word analogy sets but lagged on E-KAR. Concept-mapping accuracy for GPT-4 about 65% average in the extracted figure text (zero-shot) and about 68% with 1-shot; ChatGPT and InstructGPT lower. Providing background and explanations helped.
limits: Numbers read from garbled figure text; treat as approximate. Human comparison on the relation test used two undergraduates.
agent_relevance: Typed correspondence lists need a check; model-written mappings are right roughly two times in three at best.

source: Musker et al. (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning, Journal of Memory and Language
finding: On new tasks mapping words to letter or symbol sequences, the best LLM matched humans across conditions and beat them on the compositional variants where humans did worst. LLMs were more affected by question order and by irrelevant semantic distractors than humans were.
numbers: Study 1: LLMs more sensitive to order and distractors. Study 2: best LLM matched humans in all conditions. Brown in-person students outperformed Prolific online subjects in nearly all conditions; one target domain showed a human-specific failure mode. Exact accuracies not extracted.
limits: Exact percentages not captured; only the stated pattern is recorded. Human sample mixes two populations.
agent_relevance: Distractors with the wrong content hurt LLM mapping; strip or label irrelevant content before mapping (input hygiene).

source: Hu, Storks, Lewis & Chai (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Encoding Raven's matrix attributes as language lets a PLM do zero-shot rule induction above human level on two grid sub-tasks. Higher-level abstraction and decomposing into separate prompts help.
numbers: RAVEN: 2x2Grid 78.0% and 3x3Grid 86.4% without decomposition; 87.8% and 93.2% with layout naming and decomposition. GPT-3 175B Center up to 77.2%, rising with size. Smaller models gained from naming (125M from 22.2% to 45.6%).
limits: Synthetic perceptual puzzles; rule completion, not transfer across domains.
agent_relevance: Abstracting inputs into named relations before mapping helps. This is what a typed relation list does.

source: Synthesis of the Lewis & Mitchell / Hodel & West / Webb debate on why LLM analogy fails when surface form changes
finding: Competing explanations for LLM analogy success: (a) training-data similarity; (b) real abstraction limited by mechanical weaknesses such as counting. Experiments that separate them: counterfactual alphabets (support a), code execution fixing the counting problem (supports b), comprehension checks (rule out misunderstanding).
numbers: Humans stayed at about .75 on altered alphabets; GPT-4 .452 without code. With code GPT-4 reached about human level (Webb 2024).
limits: Neither side ran a test that blocks both explanations. Models differ across papers.
agent_relevance: The scaffold should not depend on unaided analogy; use code to compute mappings and verify on altered surface forms.
